\coursesection{01}{AI, machine learning, deep learning}{Three terms the press uses interchangeably. They are nested.}

\framekicker{Section 1.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Three nested circles, not three synonyms}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/book/figure-1-1.png}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Figure 1.1 --- deep learning is a subfield of machine learning, which is a subfield of AI.~\textcolor{ink3}{\footnotesize---~Chollet \& Watson, \emph{Deep Learning with Python}, 3rd ed. (Manning)}\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The nesting is the whole point: every deep learning system is a machine learning system, and every machine learning system is an AI system -- \hilite{but not the other way round}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{\ldots{}and one branch that sits outside machine learning}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch01-scope.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Symbolic AI is inside AI but outside machine learning. Shallow learning is inside machine learning but outside deep learning.\par}
\end{frame}
\note{This is the slide people photograph. Leave it up while you talk through the next two.}

\framekicker{Section 1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Symbolic AI: what it was, and where it stopped}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{Artificial intelligence} was born in the 1950s. The working definition: \textit{the effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans}.\par}\vskip 4pt
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}For roughly thirty years the dominant approach was \textbf{symbolic AI}: programmers wrote the rules by hand, and the machine executed them.\par}\vskip 4pt

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{minipage}[t]{1.0\textwidth}
\begin{icardgood}
\cardh{Where it worked}
Well-defined, logical problems. Chess is the canonical win.
\end{icardgood}
\end{minipage}%


\vskip 4pt

\begin{minipage}[t]{1.0\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{Where it collapsed}
\textbf{Fuzzy} problems -- recognising an image, understanding speech. Nobody can write down those rules, because nobody is aware of using them.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%

\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[signal]
Machine learning rose from the 1990s onward precisely because \hilite{the fuzzy problems were the ones left over}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The question that opened the field, in 1843}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.}\quotecite{Ada Lovelace, 1843 --- on Charles Babbage's machine}
\end{iquote}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Lovelace's objection is the oldest question in the field, and it is not rhetorical: \textbf{can a machine ever produce something we did not put into it?}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{\ldots{}and the claim that answered it, in 1956}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{Every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.}\quotecite{John McCarthy et al., the Dartmouth workshop proposal, 1956}
\end{iquote}
\begin{iband}[signal]
These two statements are 113 years apart and they disagree. Machine learning is a \textbf{partial} answer to Lovelace: the machine does produce something we never wrote down -- \hilite{the rules}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}
\note{Connect forward to the audit question that always comes up later: if we did not write the rule, who is accountable for it?}

\coursesection{02}{The inversion}{What used to be the output becomes the input.}

\framekicker{Section 1.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Machine learning runs programming backwards}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch01-paradigm.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Figure 1.2 --- classical programming is fed rules and data and emits answers; machine learning is fed data and answers and emits rules.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The consequence people underestimate}
\begin{iband}[signal]
A machine learning system is \textbf{trained, not programmed}. If you have no worked examples, there is \hilite{nothing to train}, no matter how good the architecture is.
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}This is why the hardest part of most projects turns out to be the dataset rather than the model. Chapter 6 is devoted to that problem.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Three things every ML system needs}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{1 $\cdot$ Input data points}
Sound files for speech recognition; photographs for image tagging. This is what gets transformed.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{2 $\cdot$ Examples of expected output}
Human transcripts for the sound files; tags such as \textit{dog} or \textit{cat} for the pictures.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardaccent}
\cardh{3 $\cdot$ A way to measure quality}
The distance between what the algorithm currently says and what it should say. This is the \textbf{feedback signal}.
\end{icardaccent}
\end{minipage}%
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}That adjustment step, driven by the feedback signal, is \hilite{exactly what the word \textit{learning} means here}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The three, drawn as one pipeline}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch01-ingredients.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont All three feed the same adjustment step. Remove any one of them and the arrow into it disappears.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Lose one, and it stops being machine learning}
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2256\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.282\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.4324\textwidth}}
\thead{Missing ingredient} & \thead{What you actually have} & \thead{What follows} \\ \midrule
Expected outputs & Raw data with no labels & Not supervised learning. Either label it, or move to unsupervised or self-supervised methods. \\
A quality measure & Data and labels, no agreed metric & The model can be trained but \textbf{not judged} --- and this is the most common way real projects fail. \\
Representative inputs & Examples unlike production conditions & It works on the laptop and fails in the field. Chapters 5 and 6 give this its proper names. \\
\end{itable}
\end{frame}
\note{Ask the room to test one of their own use cases against all three. The third one is missing far more often than people expect.}

\framekicker{Section 1.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Representation: the idea that runs through the whole book}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A \textbf{representation} is simply a different way of encoding the same data. The same photograph can be encoded as RGB or as HSV -- identical content, different axes.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{ibullets}
\item \textit{Select all red pixels} --- easy in \textbf{RGB}.
\item \textit{Make the image less saturated} --- easy in \textbf{HSV}.
\end{ibullets}

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Same picture, same task difficulty changed entirely. So machine learning is \hilite{the search for a representation that makes the task easy}
\end{iband}

\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.4 $\cdot$ figures 1.3--1.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The worked example: change the axes, and the rule appears}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{Raw data.} White points and black points scattered in an (x, y) plane. No simple rule separates them.
\item \textbf{Coordinate change.} Move the origin, rotate the axes. Nothing about the data changed -- only how it is written down.
\item \textbf{Better representation.} The rule is now one sentence: \textit{black points are those with x > 0}.
\end{isteps}
\begin{iband}[signal]
No model got smarter. Only the representation changed -- and that is the work that used to be called \hilite{feature engineering} and was done by hand.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why hand-written rules do not scale}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}We designed that coordinate change ourselves. Fine for a toy. But could you write explicit image transformations that separate a 6 from an 8, or a 1 from a 7, \hilite{across every kind of handwriting}\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardwarn}
\cardh{Possible --- up to a point}
Rules such as \textit{count the closed loops}, or vertical and horizontal pixel histograms, do a decent job on handwritten digits.
\end{icardwarn}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{But brittle, and miserable to maintain}
Every new handwriting sample that breaks your carefully reasoned rules forces a new transformation and a new rule --- \textbf{and you must check it against every rule you already wrote}.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Hypothesis space: what the algorithm is allowed to search}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Machine learning algorithms are \textbf{not creative} about finding these transformations. They search a predefined set of operations -- and that set is called the \textbf{hypothesis space}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
In the two-dimensional example, the hypothesis space was \hilite{the space of all possible coordinate changes}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Choosing a model architecture, in later chapters, is exactly the act of choosing a hypothesis space.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The whole field, in one sentence}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{Machine learning is searching for useful representations and rules over some input data, within a predefined space of possibilities, using guidance from a feedback signal.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 1.4}
\end{iquote}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}That one idea covers a startling range of tasks -- from autonomous driving to answering questions in natural language.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\coursesection{03}{The "deep" in deep learning}{Not deeper understanding. Just more layers.}

\framekicker{Section 1.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{"Deep" is a statement about architecture, nothing more}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{The "deep" in "deep learning" isn't a reference to any kind of deeper understanding achieved by the approach; rather, it stands for this idea of successive layers of representations.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 1.5}
\end{iquote}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The number of layers is the model's \textbf{depth}. Modern networks run to tens or hundreds of them.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}
\note{Correct the most common misconception in the room right here: 'deep' does not mean the machine understands anything more deeply.}

\framekicker{Section 1.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Each layer moves the data one step closer to the answer}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch01-layers.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Figures 1.5--1.6 --- a four-layer network for digit classification. Intermediate representations get further from the pixels and closer to the answer.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Chollet calls this \textbf{information distillation}: irrelevant information is filtered out, relevant information is amplified. All the layers are learned \hilite{at once, automatically}, from the training data.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Two better names the field never adopted}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{ibullets}
\item \textit{layered representations learning}
\item \textit{hierarchical representations learning}
\end{ibullets}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Either would have been more accurate. \textbf{Deep} won on history, not on precision.\par}\vskip 4pt

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{iband}[amber]
Its opposite has a name too: \textbf{shallow learning}, which learns only one or two layers of representation -- for instance a pixel histogram followed by a classification rule.
\end{iband}

\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\coursesection{04}{How deep learning actually works}{Three figures, and not one equation.}

\framekicker{Section 1.6 $\cdot$ figure 1.7}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Step 1 --- weights parameterise what a layer does}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}What a layer does to its input is stored in its \textbf{weights}, which are just numbers. They are also called the layer's \textbf{parameters}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
Learning, then, means \hilite{finding values for every weight} such that the network maps its example inputs to their correct targets. A large network has tens of millions of them.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.6 $\cdot$ figure 1.8}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Step 2 --- the loss function measures how far off you are}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The \textbf{loss function} takes the network's prediction and the true target, and computes a distance score. It is also called the \textit{objective function} or \textit{cost function}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
That single number is the entire feedback signal. \hilite{Everything the network learns, it learns from that one score.}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.6 $\cdot$ figure 1.9}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Step 3 --- backpropagation turns the score into an adjustment}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The loss score is used as a feedback signal to nudge the weights in the direction that lowers the loss a little. This adjustment is the job of the \textbf{backpropagation algorithm}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[amber]
The weights start out \textbf{random}, so the first outputs are nonsense and the first loss is high. What makes it work is \hilite{repetition of the loop}, not a lucky starting point.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.6}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The three figures, joined into one loop}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch01-loop.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Figures 1.7--1.9 combined: weights parameterise the layer, the loss scores the prediction against the target, and the optimizer uses that score to move the weights.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}This is called the \textbf{training loop}, repeated over thousands of examples. Chapter 2 takes every box in this picture apart.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Teaching prop $\cdot$ 1 of 3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The same loop, small enough to read in one sitting}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Chapter 1 carries no code. But the entire diagram above fits in a few lines of NumPy, and seeing it run removes any suspicion that something magical is going on.\par}\vskip 4pt
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}We generate data from a law we choose -- \inlinecode{y = 2x + 1} -- and then \hilite{throw the law away}. The program never sees it. The question is whether it can recover it.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{setup --- data from a law we then hide}{listings/ch01-01.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch01-02.txt}
\end{frame}
\note{Run it live if you can. Point out that nothing in the code contains the numbers 2 and 1.}

\framekicker{Teaching prop $\cdot$ 2 of 3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Four lines that are the three figures}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Each numbered comment below points at one of the three figures we just walked through. Nothing else is happening.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{the training loop itself}{listings/ch01-03.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Forward pass, loss, gradient, update. \hilite{Every training loop in this book is that shape}, however large the model gets.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Teaching prop $\cdot$ 3 of 3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What comes out is the rule itself}
\ioutput{listings/ch01-04.txt}
\begin{iband}[signal]
The weights travel from random to \hilite{W $\approx$ 2, b $\approx$ 1} -- the law that generated the data, which we never wrote down. That is \textit{rules as output} from figure 1.2, made concrete.
\end{iband}
\begin{ibullets}
\item Not one line told the program the answer was 2 and 1.
\item It was given only \textbf{data, answers, and a measure of loss} --- the three required ingredients.
\item Chapter 2 swaps this NumPy for tensors and automatic differentiation. The shape of the loop \hilite{does not change}.
\end{ibullets}
\end{frame}

\coursesection{05}{Why deep learning won}{Three properties, and one change that left the alternatives behind.}

\framekicker{Section 1.7}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Property 1 --- simplicity}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Deep learning automates what used to be the most crucial step in the workflow: \textbf{feature engineering}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{Shallow learning} transformed the input into one or two representation spaces -- not expressive enough for most problems. So humans went to great lengths to hand-engineer good representations first.\par}\vskip 4pt

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Deep learning learns \textbf{all} the features in one pass. Elaborate multistage pipelines get replaced by \hilite{a single, end-to-end model}
\end{iband}

\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.7}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Property 2 --- scalability}
\begin{ibullets}
\item Highly amenable to \textbf{parallelisation on GPUs} and specialised hardware, so it rides Moore's law directly.
\item Trained by iterating over \textbf{small batches}, which means dataset size is \hilite{no longer an upper bound}.
\item The only real bottleneck is available parallel compute --- and that barrier keeps moving.
\end{ibullets}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.7}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Property 3 --- versatility and reusability}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Unlike most earlier approaches, a deep learning model can be trained on \textbf{additional data without restarting from scratch} -- which makes continuous online learning viable for large production models.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
Trained models are also \textbf{repurposable}. That is the idea behind \hilite{foundation models}: very large models trained on enormous data, reusable across many new tasks with little retraining, or none.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.7}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The cost of that power}
\begin{iband}[amber]
The property that makes it strong -- \textbf{representations it discovers for itself} -- is exactly the property that makes it hard to explain. Chapter 10 returns to this for image models.
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}In regulated settings, explainability is not an academic preference. It is a requirement, and it has to be designed for rather than retrofitted.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\coursesection{06}{The age of generative AI}{What changed in 2022, and what actually made it possible.}

\framekicker{Section 1.8}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Self-supervised learning removed the labelling bottleneck}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Generative models learn to \textbf{reconstruct} the content fed into them: recover a sharp image from a noisy one, predict the next word in a sentence.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
So the targets are taken \textbf{from the input itself}. That is \hilite{self-supervised learning}, and it is what lets these models use vast amounts of \textit{unlabelled} data.
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Doing away with manual annotation -- the bottleneck of every earlier generation of machine learning -- unlocked a scale never seen before.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.8}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The scale that resulted}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.241\textwidth}
\istat{10$^{1}$$^{1}$}{order of parameters in a foundation model}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.241\textwidth}
\istat{> 1 PB}{order of training data}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.241\textwidth}
\istat{\$10s M}{order of cost to train one}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.241\textwidth}
\istat{2022}{the year it entered public awareness}
\end{minipage}%
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}These models behave like a \textbf{fuzzy database of human knowledge}. Because they have already memorised so much, they solve new problems by \textbf{prompting} -- no special-purpose programming, no retraining.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[amber]
It is newer in public attention than in research: the earliest text generation experiments date to the \textbf{1990s}, and the first edition of this book, in 2017, already had a chapter on generative models.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\coursesection{07}{What has actually been achieved}{The record, before the argument about the forecasts.}

\framekicker{Section 1.9}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Three waves in a single decade}
\begin{center}

\coursesection{08}{Beware the short-term hype}{Twice before, the field promised too much and lost its funding.}

\framekicker{Section 1.10}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What was promised in 2023, and what happened}
\begin{ibullets}
\item Soon after GPT-4, pundits claimed \textbf{nobody would need to work} and that mass unemployment was a year away.
\item Others promised economic productivity would rise \textbf{10$\times$ to 100$\times$}.
\item Two years later: US unemployment remains low, and productivity is far from any such explosion.
\end{ibullets}
\begin{iband}[signal]
To be fair to the technology: by mid-2025 generative AI was earning \textbf{tens of billions of dollars a year} -- extremely impressive for an industry that \hilite{did not exist three years earlier}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.11}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The gap that has to close somehow}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\istat{> \$200 bn}{annual AI investment, mostly data centres and GPUs}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\istat{$\approx$ \$30 bn}{annual revenue generated against it}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{AI is currently being judged by executives and investors not by what it has accomplished, but by what we are told it might soon become able to do --- much of which will durably stay out of reach of existing technologies. Something will have to give.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 1.11}
\end{iquote}
\end{frame}
\note{These are the book's figures, and they are the ones to quote in a budget meeting --- not the \$100bn/\$10bn numbers circulating elsewhere.}

\framekicker{Section 1.10}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The order is the opposite of what people assume}
\leadpar{It is tempting to think the practical success of generative AI produced the belief in near-term AGI. \hilite{It was the other way round}}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{2013} --- fears among tech elites that AGI was a few years out. The candidate was \textbf{DeepMind}, a London startup later acquired by Google.
\item \textbf{2015} --- that belief drove the founding of \textbf{OpenAI}, intended as an open-source counterweight to DeepMind.
\item \textbf{2016} --- OpenAI's recruiting pitch was that it would achieve \textbf{AGI by 2020}. Only a minority in the industry believed that timeline.
\item \textbf{Early 2023} --- a significant fraction of Bay Area engineers were convinced AGI was one or two years away.
\end{isteps}
\begin{iband}[amber]
OpenAI was critical in kick-starting generative AI. So in a peculiar twist, \textbf{the belief in near-term AGI fuelled the rise of generative AI}, not the reverse.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.11}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Winter, the first time}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{Within a generation \ldots{} the problem of creating "artificial intelligence" will substantially be solved.}\quotecite{Marvin Minsky, 1967}
\end{iquote}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{In from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being.}\quotecite{Marvin Minsky, 1970}
\end{iquote}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}When those expectations failed to materialise, researchers and government funding turned away, and the \textbf{first AI winter} began.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.11}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Winter, the second time --- and where we are now}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{The 1980s: expert systems.} A few early successes triggered a wave of investment; by around 1985 companies were spending \textbf{over \$1 billion a year}.\par}\vskip 4pt
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}By the early 1990s these systems had proven expensive to maintain, difficult to scale, and limited in scope. Interest died.\par}\vskip 4pt

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{iband}[signal]
\textbf{Now.} Chollet's own view: a full-scale retreat like the 1990s is unlikely -- AI has already demonstrated world-changing value. \hilite{If there is a winter, it should be very mild.} But some air will have to come out.
\end{iband}

\end{minipage}%
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.10}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Cognitive automation is not intelligence}
\begin{iquote}
\quotetext{Despite its name, today's "artificial intelligence" is more accurately described as "cognitive automation" --- the encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge.}\quotecite{Chollet \& Watson, section 1.10}
\end{iquote}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}It excels at problems with narrowly defined requirements, or where ample precise examples exist. It is about \textbf{enhancing the capabilities of computers}, not replicating human minds.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.10}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The cartoon and the living being}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{AI is like a cartoon character; intelligence is like a living being.} A cartoon, however realistic, can only act out the scenes it was drawn for.\par}\vskip 4pt
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textit{"If the cartoon is drawn with sufficient realism and covers sufficiently many scenes, what's the difference?"}\par}\vskip 4pt

\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
\begin{iband}[rose]
The difference is \textbf{adaptability}. Intelligence is the ability to face the unknown, adapt to it, and learn from it. Automation, even at its best, can only handle situations it has been trained on.
\end{iband}

\end{minipage}%
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}That is why building robust automation is so hard: it requires accounting for \hilite{every possible scenario}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 1.10}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What follows for anything you put into production}
\begin{iband}[rose]
If a system can only handle what it was trained on, then \textbf{monitoring for data drift is not an optional feature} -- it is a condition of the system remaining fit to use. Chapter 6 and chapter 18 return to this.
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}And the reassuring corollary: do not worry about AI suddenly becoming self-aware. Today's technology is not headed that way. \textit{"It's like expecting a better clock to lead to time travel --- they're just different things altogether."}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\coursesection{09}{The promise of AI}{The short-term forecasts deflate. The long-term change still arrives.}

\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3384\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.6016\textwidth}}

It will answer your questions and help educate your kids & Question-answering and homework assistance turned out to be the \textbf{top two} applications. \\
It will drive you from point A to point B & Fully autonomous driving is deployed at scale in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Austin. \\

\framekicker{Section 1.12}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Two things that are true at the same time}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardwarn}
\cardh{The short-term hype will deflate}
The forecasts of 2023 have not held, and the investment-to-revenue gap has to close.
\end{icardwarn}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.494\textwidth}
\begin{icardgood}
\cardh{The long-term change still comes}
Across medicine, science, industry, and daily life --- the direction was right even where the timing was wrong.
\end{icardgood}
\end{minipage}%
\begin{iband}[signal]
Holding both at once is uncomfortable, and it is \hilite{exactly what makes planning in this field difficult}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Summary}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What has to survive this chapter}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{AI $\supset$ machine learning $\supset$ deep learning.} Symbolic AI is inside AI and outside machine learning.
\item \textbf{Machine learning inverts programming}: data and answers in, rules out.
\item \textbf{Three required ingredients} --- inputs, example outputs, and a measure of quality. The third goes missing most often.
\item \textbf{"Deep" means many layers of representation}, not deeper understanding.
\item \textbf{Weights, loss, backpropagation} --- the training loop chapter 2 takes apart.
\item \textbf{The achievements are real; the forecasts have repeatedly not been.} This is cognitive automation, not yet intelligence.
\end{isteps}
